newsitem.title: USA: Search for Texas tornado victims turns up little.
newsitem.headline: Search for Texas tornado victims turns up little.

text.p: A day-long search under a hot Texas sun turned up little on Wednesday as rescue teams went over every inch of this rural community where 27 people were killed and 23 others left missing by a powerful tornado.
Dead cattle lay rotting in the torn-up fields where the twister on Tuesday mowed down 50 homes in a deadly swath four miles (6.4 km) long and half a mile (.8 km) wide.

Where the gruesome search would go next was unclear as some officials said they were nearing an end, but others vowed to push on until the missing persons were found. They said it was possible some of those unaccounted for would turn up safe, but they could not be sure.
"We assume they're still there and the search continues," said Williamson County Commissioner David Hays. "We'll expand the boundaries of the search until we find all 23."
Hays said rescue workers found only the partial remains of one person on Wednesday. "We have not found any new victims since Tuesday night," he said.
Officials said the process of identifying the badly mangled bodies would be a long and tedious one. Hopes of finding any survivors were all but gone.

"Miracles do happen in these situations but there is not much left out there. It is possible, but probably not extremely likely," said Sherri Deatherage Green, a spokeswoman with the Texas Department of Public Safety.

At least six tornadoes ripped through the heart of central Texas cn Tuesday, carrying torrential rains and baseball-sized hail. In Austin, a girl drowned in a rain-swollen creek and a man was killed when his house was struck by a tornado.

But the small town of Jarrell, which sits in rolling cattle country about 40 miles (64 km) north of Austin, suffered the worst destruction. Body parts, tattered clothes and building materials were scattered over a wide area.

Elton Bomer, chairman of Texas' State Insurance Commission, said preliminary estimates put the damage to Jarrell between $10 million and $20 million, and $25 million to $50 million for the entire area.
"I saw devastation which is hard to describe. It looked like it (the tornado) sucked the life out of the land," Gov. George Bush told reporters after he and Bomer flew over the site.
Survivors said they saw mutilated bodies of neighbors among the debris, a horse cut in two and a bull impaled on what was left of a power pole.

"One guy looked like he was 9 feet (2.7 metres) tall because his body was so stretched out," local resident Billy Williams said. "I knew these people and I could barely recognize them. It was hard to take. When I saw a dead little boy, I had to leave."

Charlie Boren said he was at home sleeping after working a night shift when his wife rushed home to get him out of the tornado's path. He ran out in his underwear and they jumped into their car and raced off, escaping death by seconds.
"I was looking right down its throat when it was about to swallow me up," Boren said.

Most of those who stayed took shelter but had nowhere to hide as the tornado, packing winds of around 200 mph (320 kph), tossed homes and trucks into the air and even sucked the asphalt off the roads.
Police said as many as 300 cattle died in the storm. Officials, worried about the stench and possible ill health effects from their bloated bodies, hauled dead animals away throughout the day.
Jarrell was hit by a tornado almost eight years ago that killed one person. But residents said Tuesday's tornado was a force of nature they hoped never to witness again.
"This one sounded like a bear growling, low tones, an evil sound," said 17-year-old Danny Williams, who took refuge with his father when the tornado passed near their home.
In all, about 200 buildings were damaged or destroyed across a four-county area by the six twisters.
Meteorologists said the Jarrell twister would most likely be categorized as an F-4 -- a devastating tornado generating winds of 207-260 mph (333-418 kph).

In human terms, the tornado is expected to rank as one of the deadliest on record in Texas. In May 1953, 114 people died when a twister devastated Waco. More recently, 42 were killed and more than 3,000 homes destroyed by an April 1979 twister that struck the city of Wichita Falls in north Texas.
